sections.text: Which at first seems like poison but afterwards acts like nectar - that pleasure is Pure, for it is born of Wisdom.
That which as first is like nectar, because the senses revel in their objects, but in the end acts like poison - that pleasure arises from Passion.
While the pleasure which from first to last merely drugs the senses, which springs from indolence, lethargy and folly - that pleasure flows from Ignorance.

So we had been discussing chapter 18, Moksha Sannyasa Yoga -- Yoga of Liberation through Renunciation. We had been discussing all throughout the chapter that this renunciation is about the sense of doership. Right now I have this sense of doership which makes me a doer.
Therefore I am bound by my own actions. But once you renounce that doership in knowledge that my true self is not the doer and therefore its all related to the actions which I perform in this life. So we have seen the entire chapter discussing the quality of actions and how the actions are performed.
It also says that if Im not attached to my actions, if I do not have ego and my Buddhi is not tainted, then even if I kill, I do not kill and Im not bound by my actions. So the bondage is because of my doership in all the actions that I perform. So therefore we have seen the physiology of action and the three things are important. Knowledge of the field actor and then the act of acting which is action itself.
These three we have discussed in detail that they are affected by the qualities of the Prakriti. Prakriti we normally translate in English as nature. So you can apply that. What is the nature of my knowledge, nature of my actions and nature of my own self will affect the outcome of this actions.
And we have seen because they are part of the Prakriti, they are affected by the Sattva Rajasav Thomas. So the knowledge can be Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic. The Karta can be Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic.
Therefore the actions will be Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic. And then we have seen that this is driven by the Buddhi and Dhruti. What kind of actions I will perform is dependent on my Buddhi.
So I have a Sattvic Buddhi. I will be performing Sattvic actions because Buddhi is the guiding factor. Buddhi as we have seen is the Reservoir of all my experiences in memory that creates my tendencies.
The Buddhi will finally decide whether its to be done or not to be done based on what I have considered it to be. My duties, my past experiences, the outcomes which I had in the past -- the Buddhi, depending on my past experiences and their outcomes, can be Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic. No action can be successful unless there is dhruti, fortitude, persistent efforts.
So what kind of a Dhruti I have will also be affecting my outcome of my actions. So we have seen that dhruti, the fortitude or grit can also be of three types. Even the person who is trying to rob a bank, he also need the fortitude.
You know, he may fail. One time he goes there first time he figures out that this is not the right time. He goes back again and again till he finds the right time to rob the bank.
So this Dhruti also can be of a Rajasik, Satvik or Tamasic. We have seen that these five are connected -- three causes of actions and two supporters: the Buddhi and Dhruti, which make the action possible. They all can be Sattvik, Rajasik or Tamasic.
Now you can see the permutation combinations of all this. There are myriads of variations of actions that we see in this world. But the reason we all act is one and the same.
We all want happiness. So this Sukha which comes out of these actions can also be of three types. Now Sukha can be translated in English as comfortable -- Im comfortable, Im a Sukhi.
Im a Dukhi -- unhappy or not comfortable. So Sukha is either comfort or joy or happiness. Any of these words can be associated with the word Sukha.
In Sanskrit there are two words: Sukha and Ananda. What is the difference between Sukha and Ananda is what we obviously were trying to figure out. But in this case it says Sukha is the goal for all my actions.
Because Sukha I associate with happiness. Comfort I associate with happiness. The word Sukha originated from the word for the space for the axle in a chariot. Su means good, kha means space.
Sukham -- good space for the axle of the chariot. Duhkham -- not so good space. In other words, if the hole in that chariot wheel is perfectly round, it is Sukham.
If it is not perfectly round, it is Duhkham. The ride will be comfortable if the axle is perfectly balanced in its space and there is no room for it to wobble. Then your ride will be comfortable.
So that comfortable ride is associated with Sukham. Duhkham will be a not very comfortable ride because the space for the axle is not perfect. So this sukhum is associated with comfort that I experience in life.
So the comfort actually relates to the outside environment. If temperature is right in this room, it is comfortable. Temperature is too high or too low, somebody will start complaining.
So it relates to the outside condition. My happiness or my comfort is dependent on the outside environment. That Sukham is generally associated with your outside conditions.
I was watching one of these interviews with Bill Gates and somebody asked him, Do you relate your wealth with happiness? And he said, Yes, I think wealth does give happiness. I dont have to worry about health care costs or anything like that. He right away related that to other peoples problems, because their conditions are not as comfortable as his. It is because of his wealth that he didnt have to worry about the normal things people have to worry about.
So Sukha is typically about the outside condition. Joy or Ananda is the state of mind. Happiness is a state of mind.
It can exist in a Sukhi or Dukhi condition. The outside condition may not be comfortable, but I may still be happy. Sukha and Duhkha, when they relate to the body, mind, and intellect, are obviously related to the outcome of my efforts.
So this verse defines three types of Sukha which are the results of my actions. Sukha also can be of three types. Im acting in this world so that my life is comfortable and I achieve happiness.
Why do you want to be comfortable? Because I want to be happy. In the end its all about happiness. We know happiness is a state of mind.
Somehow if my mind feels that its the perfect condition then it will be happy. Till that time it will keep complaining. I may have the best car, but thats not the car I wanted.
I wanted something else. Well, Im not really happy. Sukham Tvidanim Trividham Shrunu Me Bharatarshabha.
Listen, Sukha can be of three types. Sukha is also not common to all. Our standard example is smoking.
That which gives Sukha to one person, gives the guy sitting next to him discomfort. So Sukha is also personal, depending on my tendencies and my likings and my dislikings. Abhyasad Ramate Yatra Duhkhantam Cha Nigacchati.
But if you practice properly, this Sukha can lead to the end of Duhkha. If you figure out what is the cause of your Duhkha and work towards it, Sukha leads to the end of Duhkha. Thats all this verse says.
The verse says there are three types of Sukha. And if youre intelligent enough to find out what is the cause of your Duhkha, then you can end that Duhkha. But my problem is something else, and Im working on something else.
Its like having a stomach ache but hitting my head. If the cause of my Duhkha is something else but I keep trying to fix other things, it will not help. Therefore he said Abhyasat Ramate Yatra Duhkhantam Cha Nigacchati.
With constant practice of figuring out what Duhkha is and how to avoid it, Bhagavan Buddha finally figured out what the cause of all these Duhkhas in this world is. He said, well, no matter what the situation, everybodys unhappy -- somebodys sick, somebodys old, somebodys poor. And he finally found one universal cause for all Duhkha.
He said desire is the cause for all Duhkha. If you get rid of desire, all Duhkha will go away. So Bhagavan said, you should understand the nature of Sukha also.
Just because it is comfortable, it will not give you happiness. Yat Agre Visham Eva Pariname Amritopamam Tatsukham Sattvikam Proktam Atma Buddhi Prasadajam. Every word is important here to understand.
So it says that Sattvic Sukha is that which is compared to poison (Visham) in the beginning -- so difficult, like climbing Mount Everest. I dont know why people do it. I have never figured it out.
Something which you consider Sukha, and if you want to achieve that, you have to go through hell. The road to heaven passes through hell. Bhagavan said that which is in the beginning like poison but in the end like nectar -- that is Sattvic Sukha.
But where does it come from? It says Atma Buddhi Prasadajam. It comes as a Prasad from your Buddhi which is established in yourself. One who has realized his own true nature -- that Buddhi will give you a Prasad.
As we use the word Prasad in our day-to-day language, when you go to the temple and do puja, at the end there is a Prasad. Now this Prasad is not really guaranteed by my efforts. Because its up to the pujari -- whatever the Prasad, whether I get a banana or a mango.
Meena said that her eye was on the mango. But then the pujari asked the first person, Whatever fruit you want, take one from here. That person took the mango. If you are given a choice, its not really Prasad.
Prasad is to be given. Used to say, you go to the temple and just accept the Prasad. Prasad is to be given, never taken.
Prasad is something which is not in my control. It comes as a result of my efforts automatically. So that Prasad of integrating my Buddhi with the truth -- what comes out of it is the Prasad of that integration.
So the Buddhi which is established in the self, which gives you Prasad in the form of Sukha and bliss -- Bhagavan says thats Sattvic Sukha. But to get to that point was like poison. All the efforts that you put in to figure out what your true self is, going through all the experiences in life.
When Buddha went through all these experiences in his life, he went from one teacher to another. He left his kingdom, left his wife, left his child, meditated for years. Finally, under the Bodhi tree, he realized what the real nature of the truth is.
Then he achieved the bliss. Bhagavan said that the Sukha which is obtained after vigorous efforts gives the most satisfaction. Because if you earned your Sukha, then that will give you the most happiness.
If you have come to that final point of integrating your mind and intellect so that they recognize yourself, that Sukha will be permanent. And therefore it is Sattvic. In contrast to that: Vishayendriya Samyogat Yat Tad Agre Amritopamam, Pariname Visham Iva Tat Sukham Rajasam Smritam.
But that which is very pleasant in the beginning, because it is born out of contact of sense organs with the sense objects -- nice silky clothes, a nice bed -- those things give you happiness because of the contact of the sense organs with the sense objects, which feels like nectar in the beginning.

These verses present the profound teaching on the three types of happiness. Sattvic sukha (verse 37) is like poison in the beginning but nectar in the end - it arises from atma-buddhi-prasada, the clarity and grace of an intellect established in the Self. The metaphor is perfect: spiritual discipline, study, and self-inquiry can feel arduous initially, but they lead to lasting fulfillment. Rajasic sukha (verse 38) is the opposite - like nectar at first when senses contact sense objects, but poison in the end. This describes most worldly pleasures: immediately gratifying but ultimately depleting.
The word sukha itself is revealing - it originally meant good space for the chariot axle, creating a smooth, comfortable ride. Duhkha is bad space - a rough, uncomfortable journey. Sukha relates to external conditions, while ananda (bliss) is an inner state independent of circumstances. We constantly confuse the two, seeking lasting happiness through adjusting external conditions rather than establishing inner stability.
Today, observe your pursuit of happiness: Are you seeking sattvic sukha that builds over time, or rajasic sukha that provides immediate gratification but leaves you emptier than before? Notice one pleasure you regularly pursue and honestly assess its trajectory - does it lead to greater peace or greater craving? Challenge yourself to choose one sattvic practice that feels difficult now - meditation, study, discipline - and commit to it not for immediate pleasure but trusting that it becomes like nectar over time. The teaching promises that what seems like poison initially transforms into lasting fulfillment.
